reasoning: The package follows standard AUR practices with pinned, checksummed sources from Slack's official CDN. The sed patching of app.asar to modify WebRTCPipeWireCapturer is a legitimate packaging workaround for Wayland screen sharing compatibility, not malicious injection—it serves a stated purpose and doesn't introduce external code or exfiltration. The wrapper script and nvchecker config are standard. No dangerous code executes during makepkg sourcing.
disagreement_analysis: The qwen model had API errors (HTTP 400) preventing review of .nvchecker.toml and slack.sh, leading to an inconclusive verdict. It also initially flagged the app.asar patching as UNSAFE (supply-chain risk) before self-correcting to SAFE on second look. The deepseek model successfully reviewed all files and correctly identified the patching as routine packaging modification. The disagreement stems from technical failures and initial overreaction to binary patching, not genuine security concerns.
coverage_issues: qwen model failed to review .nvchecker.toml and slack.sh due to API errors (HTTP 400 BadRequestError)
false_positives: qwen model's initial UNSAFE verdict for app.asar patching: binary modification for Wayland compatibility is a legitimate AUR practice when it serves a stated purpose and doesn't inject external code
learnings: Models overreact to binary patching operations without evaluating whether they serve a stated packaging purpose—prompt should clarify that modifying upstream binaries for Linux compatibility is legitimate when checksummed and purposeful
API errors in file review should not force inconclusive verdicts when other models have successfully audited the same package—implement fallback logic to use complete audits from other models

Distinguish between 'unconventional but legitimate' packaging practices (like sed-patching ASAR files) and actual injection risks—the threat model test (does it serve no stated purpose?) should be more prominently applied
